source_text: Novimus plane et hic suspiciones eorum. Revera enim suspicantur apostolum Paulum, in secunda ad Corinthios, eidem fornicatori veniam dedisse, quem in prima dedendum Satanae in interitum carnis pronuntiarit, impium patris de matrimonio haeredem; quasique ipsum postea stylum verterit scribens: Si quis autem contristavit, non me contristavit, sed ex parte, ne vos onerem omnes. Satis est talis increpatio quae a multis fit. Uti e contrario magis vos donare et advocare, ne forte abundantiore tristitia devoretur ejusmodi. Propter quod oro vos, constituatis in eum dilectionem. In hoc enim et scripsi, uti cognoscam probationem vestram quod in omnibus obauditis mihi. Si cui autem donaveritis, et ego. Nam et ego si quid donavi, donavi in persona Christi, ne fraudemur a Satana: quoniam non ignoramus injectiones ejus. Quid hic de fornicatore, quid de paterni thori contaminatore, quid de christiano ethnicorum impudentiam supergresso intelligitur? cum proinde utique speciali venia absolvisset, quem speciali ira damnasset. Obscurius miseretur, quam indignatur; apertior est in austeritate, quam in lenitate: atquin facilius ira quam indulgentia obliqua est; magis tristiora cunctantur, quam laetiora. De modica scilicet indulgentia agebatur; quae si forte nunc aestimaretur, quando maxima quaeque non soleant etiam sine praedicatione donari, tanto abest sine significatione. Et tu quidem poenitentiam moechi ad exorandam fraternitatem in ecclesiam inducens, conciliciatum et concineratum cum dedecore et horrore compositum prosternis in medium ante viduas, ante presbyteros, omnium lacinias invadentem, omniunt vestigia lambentem, omnium genua detinentem, inque cum hominis exitum quantis potes misericordiae inlecebris, bonus pastor et benedictus Papa concionaris, et in parabola ovis, capras tuas quaeris, tua ovis ne rursus de grege exiliat, quasi non exinde jam liceat quod nec semel licuit, caeteras etiam metu comples, cum maxime indulgens. Apostolus vero sceleratam libidinem fornicationis incesto onustam tam projecte ignovisset, ut nec hunc saltem habitum legatum poenitentiae quem ab ipso didicisse deberes, ab eo exegerit, nihil de postero sit comminatus, nihil de caetero allocutus? Quin imo, et ultro obsecrat, constituerent in cum dilectionem, quasi satisfaciens, non quasi ignoscens: et tamen dilectionem audio, non communicationem. Quod et ad Thessalonicenses: Si quis autem non obaudit sermoni nostro per epistolam, hunc notate, nec commisceamini illi, ut revereatur, non quasi inimicum deputantes, sed quasi fratrem objurgantes. Adeo potuisset dicere et fornicatori dilectionem solummodo concessam, non et communicationem. Incesto vero nec dilectionem, quem scilicet auferri jussisset de medio ipsorum, multo magis utique de animo. Sed verebatur ne fraudarentur a Satana circa ejus personae amissionem, quem Satanae ipse projecerat; aut ne abundantia moeroris devoraretur, quem in interitum carnis addixerat. Hic jam carnis interitum in officium poenitentiae interpretantur, quod videatur jejuniis et sordibus et incuria omni et dedita opera malae tractationis carnem exterminando satis Deo facere; ut ex hoc argumententur fornicatorem, imo incestum illum, non in perditionem Satanae ab Apostolo traditum, sed in emendationem, quasi postea veniam ob interitum, id est conflictationem carnis, consecuturum, igitur et consecutum. Plane idem apostolus Hymenaeum et Alexandrum Satanae tradidit, ut emendarentur non blasphemare, sicut Timotheo suo scribit. Sed et ipse datum sibi ait sudem, angelum Satanae, a quo colaphizaretur ne se extolleret.. Si et hoc tangunt ut traditos Satanae ab illo, in emendationem, non in perditionem intelligamus, quid simile blasphemia et incestum et anima ab his integra, imo non aliunde quam ex summa sanctitate et ex omni innocentia elata, quae in apostolo colaphis si forte cohibebatur, per dolorem, ut aiunt, auriculae vel capitis. Incestum vero atque blasphemia totos homines in possessionem ipsi Satanae, non angelo ejus tradidisse meruerunt. Et de hoc enim interest, imo et ad hoc plurimum refert, quod illos traditos ab Apostolo legimus Satanae; Apostolo vero angelum datum Satanae. Postremo, cum deprecatur Dominum Paulus, quid audit? Satis habe gratiam meam; virtus enim in infirmitate perficitur. Hoc, qui Satanae deduntur, audire non possunt. Hymenaei autem et Alexandri crimen si et in isto et in futuro aevo irremissibile est, blasphemia scilicet; utique Apostolus non adversus terminum Domini sub spe veniae dedisset Satanae, jam a fidei in blasphemiam mersos. Unde et naufragos eos juxta fidem pronuntiavit, non habentes jam solatium navis Ecclesiae: illis enim venia negatur, qui de fide in blasphemiam impegerunt. Caeterum, ethnici et haeretici quotidie ex blasphemia emergunt. Sed etsi dixit: Tradidi eos Satanae, uti disciplinam acciperent non blasphemandi; de caeteris dixit qui, illis traditis Satanae, id est extra Ecclesiam projectis, crudiri haberent blasphemandum non esse. Sic igitur et incestum fornicatorem non in emendationem, sed in perditionem tradidit Satanae, ad quem jam super ethnicos delinquendo transierat, ut discerent fornicandum non esse. Denique in interitum, inquit, carnis, non, in cruciatum; ipsam substantiam damnans per quam exciderat, quae exinde jam perierat, baptismate amisso; ut spiritus, inquit, salvus sit in die Domini. Et de hoc enim quaeratur si spiritus hominis ipsius salvus erit. Ergo salvus erit spiritus tanto scelere pollutus, propter hoc perdita carne, ut salvus sit in poena. Ergo poenam sine carne censebit contraria interpretatio, si resurrectionem carnis amittimus. Superest igitur ut eum spiritum dixerit, qui in Ecclesia censetur, salvum, id est integrum, praestandum in die Domini ab immunditiarum contagione, ejecto incesto fornicatore; siquidem subjungit: Non scitis quod modicum fermentum totam desipiat conspersionem? Et tamen fornicatio incesta non erat modicum, sed grande fermentum.
pass_a_gloss: We know also their suspicions here. For they suspect that Apostle Paul, in the second to the Corinthians, gave forgiveness to the same fornicator, whom in the first he had pronounced to be handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, an impious heir of his father's marriage; and as if he himself afterwards changed his writing style, writing: If anyone has grieved, he has not grieved me, but in part, lest I burden all of you. It is enough such a rebuke as is made by many. Rather, I want to give and call you, lest perhaps he be devoured by excessive sorrow. On account of which I ask you, establish love towards him. For I wrote this, so that I may know your proof, that you obey me in all things. If you forgive anyone, I also do. For even I, if I have forgiven anything, I have forgiven in the person of Christ, lest we be cheated by Satan: for we are not ignorant of his injections. What is understood here about the fornicator, what about the contaminator of his father's marriage bed, what about the Christian who surpassed the impudence of the Gentiles? Since, accordingly, he had absolved him with special forgiveness, whom he had condemned with special anger. He has more pity obscurely than he has indignation; he is more open in austerity than in leniency: but, on the other hand, anger is more easily turned away than indulgence; more sorrowful things are hesitated over than joyful ones. It was a matter of moderate indulgence; which, if perhaps it were estimated now, when the greatest things are not usually given even without preaching, how much more without indication. And you, indeed, introducing the penitence of the adulterer to exhort the brotherhood in the church, you prostrate, composed with shame and horror, in the midst, before the widows, before the presbyters, invading the laps of all, licking the footsteps of all, detaining the knees of all, and with as much mercy as you can, you preach, good shepherd and blessed Papa, and in the parable of the sheep, you seek your goats, your sheep, lest it again go out of the flock, as if it were not already lawful what was not once lawful, you also fill the others with fear, when you are most indulgent. But did the Apostle, indeed, so openly forgive the criminal lust of fornication, laden with incest, that he did not even exact from him this habit of penitence, which he ought to have learned from him, nor did he threaten anything about the future, nor did he address anything else? Rather, he even begs that they establish love towards him, as if satisfying, not as if forgiving: and yet I hear love, not communion. Which also to the Thessalonians: If anyone does not obey our word through the epistle, note this one, and do not associate with him, that he may be ashamed, not as if appointing him an enemy, but as if rebuking a brother. So, he could have said also to the fornicator that love alone was conceded, not communion. But to the incestuous person, neither love, whom, indeed, he had ordered to be taken away from their midst, much more, indeed, from their heart. But he was afraid lest they be cheated by Satan regarding the loss of his person, whom Satan himself had cast out; or lest he be devoured by excessive sorrow, whom he had handed over to the destruction of the flesh. Here now they interpret the destruction of the flesh as a function of penitence, which seems to make satisfaction to God by means of fasts and filth and every neglect and dedication to bad treatment, exterminating the flesh; so that they argue that the fornicator, indeed, that incestuous person, was not handed over by the Apostle to Satan for destruction, but for emendation, as if he would afterwards obtain forgiveness on account of the destruction, that is, the conflict of the flesh, and therefore had obtained it. Indeed, the same Apostle handed over Hymenaeus and Alexander to Satan, that they might be emended, not to blaspheme, as he writes to his Timothy. But he himself says that a thorn was given to him, an angel of Satan, by whom he was buffeted, lest he be exalted. If, then, they touch on this, that those handed over to Satan by him are understood to be for emendation, not for destruction, what is similar between blasphemy and incest and a soul intact, indeed, not otherwise than elevated from the highest sanctity and from all innocence, which, if perhaps, was restrained in the Apostle by buffets, through pain, as they say, of the ear or head? But incest and blasphemy have handed over whole men to the possession of Satan himself, not to his angel. And it is also of interest, indeed, it pertains much to this, that we read those handed over to Satan by the Apostle; but the Apostle himself was given an angel of Satan. Finally, when Paul prays to the Lord, what does he hear? My grace is sufficient for you; for virtue is perfected in infirmity. This, those who are handed over to Satan cannot hear. But if the crime of Hymenaeus and Alexander is irremissible, even in the future age, namely blasphemy; certainly the Apostle did not hand them over to Satan against the limit of the Lord, in hope of forgiveness, already sunk in blasphemy from faith. Whence, he also pronounced them shipwrecked, according to faith, not having the solace of the ship of the Church: for forgiveness is denied to those who have sunk from faith into blasphemy. But, on the other hand, Gentiles and heretics emerge daily from blasphemy. But if he said: I handed them over to Satan, that they might receive discipline, not to blaspheme; he said about the others, who, having been handed over to Satan, that is, cast out of the Church, ought to be rebuked, not to blaspheme. So, therefore, the incestuous fornicator was not handed over to Satan for emendation, but for destruction, to whom he had already passed over, sinning beyond the Gentiles, that they might learn not to fornicate. At last, he says, to the destruction, not to the torment, of the flesh, condemning the very substance by which he had fallen, which from then on had already perished, the baptism having been lost; that the spirit may be saved, he says, in the day of the Lord. And it is asked about this, if the spirit of the man himself will be saved. Therefore, the spirit will be saved, polluted by so great a crime, on account of the lost flesh, that it may be saved in punishment. Therefore, a contrary interpretation will consider punishment without flesh, if we lose the resurrection of the flesh. It remains, therefore, that he said the spirit, which is considered in the Church, saved, that is, intact, to be presented on the day of the Lord, from the contagion of impurities, the incestuous fornicator having been cast out; for he adds: Do you not know that a little leaven corrupts the whole lump? And yet, incestuous fornication was not a little leaven, but a great one.

pass_b_english: We know their suspicions here perfectly well. They suspect that the apostle Paul, in his second letter to the Corinthians, granted forgiveness to the very same fornicator whom, in his first letter, he had handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh (1 Corinthians 5:5) — an impious heir to his father's marriage bed. They act as if Paul then changed his tune, writing: "If anyone has caused pain, he has caused it not to me, but in some measure — not to put it too severely — to all of you. For such a one, this punishment by the majority is enough. So you should rather turn to forgive and comfort him, or he may be overwhelmed by excessive sorrow. That is why I beg you to reaffirm your love for him. I wrote for this very purpose: to test you and see whether you are obedient in everything. Anyone whom you forgive, I also forgive. Indeed, what I have forgiven, if I have forgiven anything, has been for your sake in the presence of Christ, so that we would not be outwitted by Satan; for we are not ignorant of his designs" (2 Corinthians 2:5-11).

But what is actually understood here about the fornicator, about the defiler of his father's bed, about the Christian who outdid the very shamelessness of the Gentiles? Since Paul had absolved with special mercy the very man he had condemned with special wrath. His pity is obscure; his severity is open. Yet anger is more easily turned aside than indulgence; we hesitate longer over harsh things than joyful ones. We are dealing with a moderate indulgence — which, if it were assessed today, when even the greatest gifts are not usually given without proclamation, would be all the more impossible without some sign.

And you — dragging the adulterer's penance into the church to exhort the brotherhood — you throw him down in the middle, a spectacle composed of shame and horror, before widows, before presbyters, invading every lap, licking every footstep, clutching every knee. And with every lure of mercy you can muster, you preach — good shepherd, blessed Pope — and in the parable of the sheep you go hunting for your goats, pleading for your own sheep lest it wander from the flock again, as if what was never lawful even once has now become lawful. You strike the rest with fear even while you are at your most indulgent.

Yet the apostle so openly forgave the criminal lust of fornication, weighted with incest, that he did not even demand from him that habit of penance which he ought to have learned from Paul himself. He threatened nothing about the future; he addressed nothing further. On the contrary, he actually begged them to establish love toward the man, as if making satisfaction rather than granting forgiveness — and yet I hear only of love, not of communion. Paul says the same to the Thessalonians: "If anyone does not obey what we say in this letter, take note of that person, and have nothing to do with him, that he may be ashamed. Do not regard him as an enemy, but warn him as a brother" (2 Thessalonians 3:14-15). So he could have said to the fornicator that love alone was conceded, not communion. But to the incestuous man — neither love, since he had ordered him removed from their midst, much less from their hearts.

Paul feared, however, that they might be cheated by Satan over the loss of this man's person — the very man Satan himself had cast out — or that he might be swallowed by excessive sorrow, the man Paul had handed over to the destruction of the flesh (1 Corinthians 5:5). Now they reinterpret that destruction of the flesh as a penitential function: as if fasts, filth, total neglect, and dedication to abusing the body — exterminating the flesh — could satisfy God. From this they argue that the fornicator, that incestuous man, was not handed over by the apostle to Satan for destruction, but for correction — as if he would later obtain forgiveness because of that destruction, that is, the conflict of the flesh, and therefore had already obtained it.

The same apostle handed Hymenaeus and Alexander over to Satan that they might learn not to blaspheme (1 Timothy 1:20). Yet Paul himself says a thorn was given him, a messenger of Satan, to buffet him and keep him from becoming conceited. If they press this parallel — that those handed over to Satan by Paul were for correction, not destruction — what similarity exists between blasphemy and incest, and a soul kept intact, indeed elevated from the highest sanctity and all innocence, which, if restrained in the apostle at all, was restrained by buffets, through pain, as they say, of ear or head? Incest and blasphemy handed whole men over to the possession of Satan himself, not merely to his messenger. And this matters greatly: we read that those men were handed over to Satan by the apostle; but the apostle himself was given a messenger of Satan.

Finally, when Paul pleads with the Lord, what does he hear? "My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness." Those who are handed over to Satan cannot hear that. But if the crime of Hymenaeus and Alexander is irremissible even in the age to come — namely blasphemy — then certainly the apostle did not hand them over to Satan against the Lord's limit, in hope of forgiveness, men already sunk from faith into blasphemy. Therefore he pronounced them shipwrecked regarding the faith, having no comfort from the ship of the Church: for forgiveness is denied to those who have plunged from faith into blasphemy. Yet Gentiles and heretics emerge daily from blasphemy.

But if Paul said, "I handed them over to Satan that they may learn not to blaspheme" (1 Timothy 1:20), he spoke of the others — those handed over to Satan, that is, cast out of the Church — that they should be rebuked not to blaspheme. So therefore the incestuous fornicator was not handed over to Satan for correction, but for destruction — a man who had already gone beyond the Gentiles in sinning — that they might learn not to fornicate. In the end, Paul says, "for the destruction of the flesh, not for torment" — condemning the very substance by which he had fallen, which had already perished from that point on, baptism having been lost — "that his spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord" (1 Corinthians 5:5).

The question is asked: will that man's spirit itself be saved? Therefore the spirit, polluted by so great a crime, will be saved on account of the lost flesh, so that it may be saved in punishment. A contrary interpretation would have punishment without flesh, if we lose the resurrection of the flesh. It remains, then, that Paul meant the spirit which is recognized in the Church — saved, that is, kept intact, to be presented on the day of the Lord, free from the contagion of impurities, the incestuous fornicator having been cast out. For he adds: "Do you not know that a little leaven leavens the whole lump?" And yet incestuous fornication was not a little leaven, but a great one.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex theological arguments regarding the distinction between 'emendation' (emendationem) and 'destruction' (perditionem/interitum), and correctly identifies the nuances of 'love' (dilectionem) versus 'communion' (communicationem). All scripture citations (1 Cor 5:5, 2 Cor 2:5-11, 2 Thess 3:14-15, 1 Tim 1:20) are correctly applied to the relevant Latin clauses. Pass A and Pass B are consistent with the Latin source.
